1:
Why the exhortation comes here Chrysostom explains by two images. The young sailor is inspired with great confidence if the master of the ship has survived a shipwreck, and in war the captain who sees his general wounded and recovered is encouraged; so it consoles the faithful that the Apostle suffered greatly and was not made weak by it, and had it not been so he would not have related it. He puts the objection sharply: Paul has shaken his readers with terrors, told them he is in chains and forsaken, and then adds, as if he had suffered nothing, be strong. The answer is that these things were to Timothy's strengthening more than to Paul's: if I endure them, much more oughtest thou; if the master, much more the disciple. Ellicott and Barnes read the connection back into the preceding chapter, where after the faithless Asiatics and the loyal Onesiphorus Paul turns to Timothy with, imitate the one and make up for the many; Gill finds it in the illative particle.

What strength in grace means divides them predictably. Calvin states the objection himself, of what use it is to exhort a man to be strong in grace unless free will cooperate, and answers that what God demands by his word he likewise bestows by his Spirit; the exhortations are not superfluous, because the Spirit teaching us inwardly keeps them from sounding to no purpose, and whoever grants that this exhortation could not have been fruitful without the secret power of the Spirit will never support free will by it. Clarke moves the other way from the word itself: though the genuine import of grace is favour, it often implies an active principle communicated from God, light directing how to act and power to act by that light. Robertson settles it grammatically: the present passive imperative means keep on being empowered, Christ being the dynamo only while we keep in touch with him.

Henry reads the phrase as a contrast, not a definition, setting strength in the grace that is in Christ against strength in our own, and points it by Peter, who promised to die rather than deny his Lord in his own strength, and who, had he been strong in Christ's grace, would have kept his standing better. The things committed the rest take narrowly or broadly. Barnes suspects a solemn charge given before the church at Timothy's ordination, stating a summary of Christian doctrine, and Clarke the same, the form of sound words delivered when hands were laid on him. Ellicott widens it deliberately: these have often been understood as a few fundamental truths of the nature of a creed, but it is better to take them as the sum of Paul's teaching, the general conception of his theology, shrined in such epistles as those to the Romans or the Ephesians. Wesley reads the charge to commit as, before thou leavest Ephesus.

Whether the verse establishes a succession is the one open quarrel. Clarke grants that the truths continue in the Church and faithful men still proclaim them, then turns on the doctrine: where is the uninterrupted apostolical succession, and who can tell? Probably it does not exist on the face of the world, and he who appeals to it for his authority had best sit down till he has made it out. Barnes takes a middle position: the verse warrants ministers setting apart others, does not prove the people unfree to choose their own pastor, and locates the true line of succession in good men qualified to teach who have the Spirit of Christ, not merely in the ordained. Ellicott denies that it supports authoritative oral teaching, but insists the treasure be handed on unimpaired, leaving the runners to pass their torches still burning; Chrysostom requires both qualities together, since it is no advantage that a man be faithful if he cannot convey his doctrine.
3:
The soldier is the first of three pictures, and the text is disputed. Ellicott notes that the older authorities lack the words rendered thou therefore, and that the compounded verb is better rendered, take thy share in suffering; Robertson reads the same compound as a personal challenge, the old preacher asking the young one to share hardship, and observes that Paul never hesitated over this military metaphor, having called Epaphroditus and Archippus his fellow-soldiers. Barnes fills the figure in: soldiers are taken from home and friends, exposed to cold or heat or storms or fatiguing marches, sustained on coarse fare or almost destitute of food, and often sink under their burdens and die; he would make a bad soldier, Barnes adds, who at enlistment made it a condition that he sleep on a bed of down and never be exposed to peril. Gill keeps the word plain: to endure hardness is to suffer evil, meaning persecution, loss of name and goods, scourging, imprisonment and death.

What the figure forbids they draw from Roman military law, Grotius supplying it to Barnes and Clarke alike: the legionary might not marry, nor engage in husbandry or trade, nor act as tutor, curator of another's estate or proctor in another's cause, being excluded from whatever would divert him from his one pursuit. Barnes turns this on the ministry, that it is equally improper to be entangled with the business of a farm, with plans of speculation and gain, or with any purpose of worldly aggrandisement; Ellicott reports that the Catholic Church has generally read the verse as barring her ministers from secular pursuits of business or pleasure. Wesley qualifies the whole with three words, that no man entangles himself more than is unavoidable, and Robertson notes that the term for the affairs is an old word for business found only here in the New Testament.

Clarke then turns the rebuke round on the opposite fault. Many sin against this direction, he grants, loving the world and labouring for it, regardless of the souls committed to their charge; but what are they, either in number or guilt, compared to the immense herd of men professing to be Christian ministers who neither read nor study and consequently never improve? These are too conscientious to meddle with secular affairs, yet have no scruple to while away time and by their monotonous ministry become an incumbrance to the Church. He asks in what sect or party they are found and answers, in all: idle drones, born to consume the produce of the soil, who cannot teach because they will not learn. Paul's own trade Ellicott raises as the obvious objection, answering that Jewish life desired its rabbis to practise a handicraft, that missionaries could not otherwise ensure subsistence, and that such pioneers had to stand above suspicion of covetousness; but he denies the combination was ever meant as a rule, calling First Corinthians nine decisive.

Striving lawfully means more than fair play. Ellicott says it means according to the prescribed conditions of the contest, so the athlete must submit to the rules of the theatre and, if he hopes for a prize, go through the long and severe training beforehand, Galen using the same phrase of complying with the rules of diet; Barnes reports that one who transgressed the rules in the least matter not only failed of the prize, though the apparent victor, but was sometimes disgraced and punished. On the husbandman Barnes departs from the rest, preferring the marginal construction that joins first to labour, so the law is that a man must work before he reaps, which accords with the apostle's purpose of encouraging Timothy to persevere; the Greek will bear it, he grants, though it is not the most obvious construction. Ellicott lays the emphasis instead on that laboureth, and denies Theophylact's account of the closing charge, these metaphors being the reverse of obscure.
8:
Remember Jesus Christ they read as two facts, not one, and Ellicott gets there by the word order. The Greek puts of the seed of David after, not before, raised from the dead, so it should run, remember Jesus Christ as one raised from the dead, born of the seed of David: the Resurrection reminds Timothy of his Master's victory over death, the Incarnation whispers that the risen One sprang, like himself, from mortal flesh and blood, and the phrasing adds a third thing, the Messianic race of Jeremiah's righteous Branch. Barnes shifts the emphasis the same way: the point is not to reflect on the fact of the rising but to think of the Saviour himself, raised after all the sorrows of this life. Robertson keeps the perfect participle, still risen; Wesley reduces the whole to a line, that this is the one genealogy to attend to; Henry makes the resurrection the great proof of the divine mission; Clarke ties according to my gospel to the error that the resurrection was past already.

Where Paul was when he wrote Barnes cannot establish, and describes anyway. Tradition puts him with Peter in the Mamertine prison, built by Ancus Marcius and enlarged by Servius Tullius, the lower chamber once a quarry and later a granary, two apartments of uncemented stone entered only through the roof, and holding a spring said at Rome to have risen at Peter's command to baptize his keepers. No certain reliance can be placed on any of this, Barnes says, though there is no improbability in the prisons having held Christians; a more horrible place of confinement, he reports, can scarcely be conceived. Gill itemises the trouble as reproaches, persecutions, whipping, beating, stoning and imprisonment; Ellicott notes that the word rendered evil-doer is that used of the two thieves crucified with Jesus.

The turn that follows they treat as the heart of the passage. Barnes calls it one of Paul's happy turns of thought, that he is fettered and the gospel is not, so his imprisonment matters little beside the triumph of truth; Robertson puts it flatly, I am bound with a chain, but no fetters are on the word of God; Wesley glosses it, not hindered in its course; and Henry draws the inference that persecuting powers may silence and restrain ministers but cannot hinder the operation of the word upon men's hearts and consciences, so that though the preachers are often bound the word is never bound. Chrysostom sets the promise that follows against an objector judging the future from things present, who asks, when I live, I die, and when I die, I live? Thou promisest nothing on earth, and dost thou give it in heaven? He presses the condition too: not simply that we shall reign, but if we suffer, since it is not enough to die once, and the apostle himself died daily.

Whether the faithful saying is quoted they cannot settle; whether its close comforts or threatens is the real division. Ellicott judges it most likely an ancient Christian hymn, or part of a liturgy in common use, like the comfortable words of the Communion Service; Robertson allows the hymn fragment and notes four conditions all of the first class; Clarke denies there is anything to look for and rebukes Tillotson for hunting a saying of Christ kept by tradition. Wesley takes pure comfort, that though some believe not God will make good his promises to them that do. Ellicott flatly denies it: those who hear soothing voices for the sinner here are gravely mistaken, the passage being of distinct severity, perhaps among the sternest in the Book of Life, since he cannot treat the faithless as faithful. Barnes turns it on election: if it made a man safe while living in sin it would deserve all the opprobrium ever heaped upon it. Gill and Henry keep both senses at once.
14:
Strife about words they all condemn, and Clarke says why it happens. Words, not things, have been a most fruitful source of contention in the Christian world, and among religious people the chief cause of animosity has been apprehending the same term in different ways while both meant the same thing; hence preachers should explain the terms they use and never employ them in any other sense. Henry says those disposed to strive commonly strive about matters of very small moment, and that if people considered how little use most religious controversies are they would not be so zealous, since such strifes are not merely useless but hurtful, shaking some and subverting others, and endangering truth by the unchristian heats they occasion. Robertson notes that the verb was apparently coined by Paul as a back formation, and that a mere war of words displeases him; Wesley exclaims how many unnecessary things are thus unprofitably contended for.

Rightly dividing draws four pictures from one word. Clarke reports the common view, that the allusion is to the priests dividing the victim down the spine so scrupulously that half the spinal marrow lay on each side, and rejects it: nothing was farther from the apostle's thoughts, and the practice was no original ordinance among the Jews but a matter stressed only in later times. Ellicott renders it rightly laying out the word of truth, a metaphor from laying out a road, as in the Greek of Proverbs, or from drawing a furrow, whose merit is its straightness. Robertson adds Theodoret's ploughing of a straight furrow and Parry's stone mason cutting stones straight, then offers his own: Paul was a tent-maker who knew how to cut rough camel-hair cloth straight, and plenty of exegesis is crooked enough to call for it.

Whether the cutting was still felt in the word Ellicott answers against the majority. To hold with Alford and Huther-Meyer that the notion had been lost, so that by Paul's time the word meant simply to manage rightly without falsifying, seems to him premature; he grants only the later development, since Clement of Alexandria in the third century uses the noun as an equivalent for orthodoxy with the cutting gone, and suggests that Paul's own use gave the word a fresh starting-point so that the original meaning gradually passed out of sight. Wesley takes the practical sense without the philology, that it means duly explaining and applying the whole scripture so as to give each hearer his due portion, and adds that those who give one part of the gospel to all, the comforts to unawakened, hardened, scoffing men, have real need to be ashamed. Clarke ends in the same place, milk to babes and reproof to the careless.

Whether the false teaching is a cancer or a gangrene Ellicott settles by the pace of the diseases, and what the teachers held nobody can say. Cancer, which Luther also adopted, fails to express the deathly nature of their word, since a sufferer from cancer may live many years where a few hours ends the life of one attacked with gangrene unless the limb be cut away; to render the Greek by cancer is to water down the original. Gill agrees the marginal gangrene is better, Barnes explains that it spreads into the surrounding healthy parts as error eats out the truths connected with the one it touches, and Robertson notes the medical writers who use the word. Of the error itself Barnes admits the form is unknown, offering Augustine's supposition of a resurrection of the soul from the death of sin; Wesley guesses the spiritual passing from death unto life; Robertson knows nothing of Philetus; and Barnes adds that no man can safely hold a single error, any more than one part of his body in mortification.
19:
What the firm foundation is they answer six ways. Gill takes it of the faith of God's elect, which false teachers cannot overthrow as they may an historical or temporary faith, or else of the doctrine of the resurrection they denied. Henry takes it that the unbelief of men cannot make God's promise of no effect, since it is not possible they should deceive the elect, or else of the truth itself, which weathers all the storms raised against it. Barnes and Ellicott make it the Church, and Ellicott presses the word: it is called a foundation because the Church on earth is only the ground-storey of the Temple of the future, so that this life is but a beginning and the visible Church the first storey of what the Architect will complete in heaven. Clarke makes it the religion of Christ, a noble mansion; Wesley reduces it to God's truth and faithfulness.

Why the inscription is called a seal they explain from different customs. Clarke thinks of ancient temples: above the door at Delphi stood the Greek words thou art, on which Plutarch wrote a treatise, mosque walls carry sentences from the Koran, and the Jewish high priest's mitre bore Holiness to the Lord. But he prefers a second reading, that the word means a contract sealed by both parties, noting that among the Asiatics such seals scarcely ever carry image or figure but always some very expressive inscription, of which he has seen many and has several before him as he writes; so the two sentences stand on two seals, not two faces of one, where Henry and Ellicott keep a single broad seal with a motto on each side. Ellicott grounds the figure in the dedication of buildings, as on Egypt's oldest monuments, and says a seal best conveys the binding character of the writing.

Where the sentences come from Robertson traces to one episode. The first is a quotation of Numbers, the second a paraphrase of Numbers with Isaiah and Jeremiah, and he judges the whole probably another echo of the rebellion of Korah, the verb meaning let every one stand off from. Ellicott finds the second rather in the command to touch no unclean thing, spoken to those that bear the vessels of the Lord, and takes naming the name to mean that no man confessing with the heart that Jesus is Lord can deliberately commit iniquity, which here includes the teaching of those false men, since it led away from truth into a lax and evil life. Clarke notes that almost all the important manuscripts read Lord rather than Christ; Wesley draws the edge: they only are his who depart from iniquity, and to all others he will say, I know you not.

Whether the great house is the Church or the world divides them flatly. Chrysostom says the wicked are suffered to remain that they may be converted or made an example, and that Paul gives a similar case; but he insists the figure covers the world at large and not the Church only, telling his hearers plainly not to think he means the Church. Gill takes the contrary position by name: by this great house is not meant the world, as some think. Clarke keeps it to the building of the preceding verse, finding at Ephesus vessels of gold in the sincere teachers and of earth in Hymenaeus and Philetus; Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley take it of the Church, Ellicott treating it as Paul's answer to the question how so many unworthy members come to be in it. Wesley adds the qualification the others miss, that a vessel even of gold may be put to the vilest use, though that was not its maker's design. Clarke, having pressed the similes hardest, ends by confessing that the apostle never applied them, and that it is very difficult to tell what he means.
22:
Which lusts are meant they narrow at once, and Clarke dates them. Not only irregular and sensual desires, he says, but pride, ambition and above all the lust of power, to which most men will sacrifice every other propensity, their ease, pleasure and health; it is the most bewitching passion in the human heart, ruinous in Church and state but chiefly in the former. Timothy was now between thirty and forty, the very age at which ambition most prevails, since carnal pleasures are the sins of youth, ambition of middle age, and covetousness and carking cares of old age. Gill narrows them the same way, not to uncleanness or the follies of youth, to which Timothy was not inclined, but to what prevails with young ministers: vain glory, popular applause, pre-eminence, contempt of others. Henry keeps the plainer sense, adding that though Timothy was holy and mortified to the world, the best must not be secure; Robertson notes only that there are lusts peculiar to flaming youth.

What is wrong with the questions Ellicott finds hard to name. The word rendered unlearned is better rendered ignorant, since these could hardly be called unlearned, much useless learning being thrown away in the schools; they were rather pointless and stupid as well as foolish, and Robertson quotes Parry's phrase, the speculations of a half-educated mind, rendering the result bluntly, they beget battles. Barnes blames the subject matter: many questions the Greeks and Hebrews discussed pertained to points which could not be settled, or which, if settled, were of no importance. On the striving that follows Barnes states what is not forbidden: the servant of the Lord may inquire calmly after truth, discuss points of morals or theology with a proper spirit, and contend earnestly for the faith once delivered; Gill agrees that he ought to strive for the faith of the Gospel, the fault being strife about words for mastery and not truth. Wesley calls the forbidden striving the eager or passionate kind; Ellicott grounds the whole in the servant's Master, of whom Isaiah prophesied that he shall not strive nor cry.

Who the opposers are Ellicott distinguishes sharply. St Paul alludes scarcely so much to the leading teachers of false doctrine as to those led away by them: the pronounced heretics of Titus were, after a first and second admonition, to be shunned and left to themselves, whereas here nothing is said of admonitions and no hint given that these are to be shunned, their treatment being gentle. Clarke takes the opposite view, that the word means those who opposed the apostle's authority, whence the propriety of the allusion to Korah's rebellion, though bad as they were they were not beyond God's mercy. Barnes gives the rule: we are not to become angry with such persons, nor denounce them at once as heretics, nor hold them up to public reproach, but calmly to show them what the truth is, their grand difficulty being that they are ignorant of it.

The last verse none of them finds easy. Clarke calls the construction extremely difficult, sets the Greek beside the older English versions of Wiclif and Coverdale to show how differently it has been taken, and concludes that God will deal with these men as he dealt with Korah, the believers holding no communion with them and the seal being a contract between two parties each setting his own motto to it; he grants that the common interpretation will probably be followed anyway. Ellicott puts the crux precisely: the pronouns are distinct Greek words, so the first refers to the devil and the second to God; Robertson concedes only that the phrase is understood variously. On the awakening they agree, Gill, Barnes and Ellicott taking the word of a man sobering from drunkenness or roused from sleep, and Wesley noting that these are not only captives but asleep, utterly insensible of their captivity.
